title: The Tree That Bends in the Storm
blurb: The palm is not really a tree at all. It has no bark, no branches, and no rings, and it bends flat in a hurricane instead of breaking.

blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: This is a palm tree. It grows where it is warm. Its leaves are long and green. They wave in the wind. Big coconuts grow at the top. When a big wind comes, the palm tree bends. blocks.prompt: The Tree That Bends in the Storm
blocks.text: The palm tree grows by the sea. Its leaves are called fronds. A frond can be longer than a car. Wind blows on the palm tree all day long. The palm tree does not fight the wind. It bends. Its trunk is soft inside, like a big bunch of straws, so it can lean far over and not snap. Then it springs back up. Coconuts grow at the top of the palm. A coconut has a thick brown coat. The coat is full of air. If a coconut falls in the sea, it floats away.

blocks.prompt: The Tree That Is Not a Tree
blocks.text: An oak tree and a palm tree stand in the same yard, and only one of them is really a tree. The palm is the odd one. Palms are not related to oaks or pines at all. Their closest cousins are grasses, corn, and lilies. A palm is really a giant grass that learned to stand up tall. Look for the clues. An oak has bark. A palm does not. An oak has branches everywhere. A palm has none. Cut an oak trunk and you can count the rings and know its age. Cut a palm trunk and there are no rings to count, just tough fibers running up and down like a bundle of straws. An oak grows wider every year. A palm does not. A palm gets its full width first, near the ground, and then pushes straight up at the same thickness for the rest of its life. All of that growing happens in one place: a single fat bud at the very top. Palms keep their whole future in one spot.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in a full sentence.

Which plants are a palm's closest cousins?
Why can you not count rings to find out how old a palm is?
Why do you think a palm is in trouble if something damages the bud at the top?
answers: bark and branches (rings also counts)
grasses, corn, and lilies
a palm has no rings, only fibers running up and down
(inference: all of its growing happens in that one bud)

4.title: The Tree That Bends in the Storm
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Tree That Bends in the Storm

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Cocos nucifera, the coconut palm
The husk is full of air, so it floats
Coconut water is packed in for the seedling
A coconut can drift for months and still sprout
A coconut is a drupe, not really a nut
Pacific sailors carried them by canoe

blocks.prompt: The Seed That Sailed
blocks.text: A coconut is built like a boat, and that is not an accident. Start from the outside. The coconut you find on a beach is wrapped in a thick husk of dry brown fiber. That husk is packed with air pockets, which is why a whole coconut floats high in the water instead of sinking. Inside the husk sits the hard shell, sealed tight, and inside the shell is the part that matters: white meat and a cup of sweet water. That water is not seawater and it is not rain. It is food and drink the parent palm packed for the seedling, sealed in before the journey started. Now push the coconut into the sea. Currents carry it. Weeks pass, then months. Salt water cannot get in through the shell, so the seedling inside stays fresh, living off its own supply. When a wave finally rolls the coconut up onto sand somewhere far away, a shoot pushes out through a soft spot in the shell, drinks the water stored inside, and grows. Scientists have tested this. A coconut can drift for months and still sprout. This is why coconut palms lean over so many warm beaches around the world. Some of them arrived on ocean currents. Many others were carried on purpose by Pacific sailors, who packed coconuts in their canoes as water, food, rope, and roofing all in one. Between the tide and the traveler, the coconut got almost everywhere the weather was warm.

items: Explain how the husk lets a coconut float.

answers: the husk is thick fiber full of air pockets, so the coconut rides high in the water
the parent palm packed it in and sealed it before the coconut fell
(inference: it keeps salt water out so the seedling stays alive for months)
(inference: the floating design was shaped by evolution because drifting spreads the seed)

5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

meta.templateLabel: The Tree That Bends in the Storm

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: No cambium, so a palm makes no wood and no rings
Fibrous bundles set in soft tissue: cables in foam
Fronds shred and streamline in high wind
Thousands of thin roots, no taproot
A palm cannot heal a wound in its trunk
One bud on top: lose it and the palm dies

blocks.prompt: Why the Palm Bends and the Oak Breaks
blocks.text: After a hurricane passes over a warm coast, the pictures look the same every time. Oaks are down. Roofs are gone. And the palms are still standing, leaning, stripped, but rooted. People treat this as a nice metaphor about staying flexible. It is actually a physics problem, and the palm solves it differently than every tree around it. Start with the trunk. An oak trunk is a solid cylinder of wood that gets a new ring of it every year, added by a living layer called the cambium just under the bark. That design makes an oak stiff, wide, and strong. Stiff things resist a load until the moment they do not, and then they break. A palm has no cambium and no rings. Its trunk is a column of soft tissue with thousands of tough fibrous bundles threaded up through it, closer to a bundle of cables set in foam than to a block of wood. Load it sideways and it does not resist. It bends, sometimes far enough to touch its own crown to the ground, and when the wind drops it stands back up. The crown helps too. Palm fronds are cut into strips, and in high wind those strips fold back and streamline like a wet flag, spilling the air instead of catching it. A broad leaf catches wind. A shredded one does not. Palms also carry no heavy side branches for the wind to lever against, and their roots are not one thick taproot but thousands of thin ones spreading wide, which grips loose sand better than a single anchor would. Every design has a bill to pay. Because a palm has no cambium, it cannot make new wood, which means it cannot heal. Carve your name into an oak and the tree grows over it. Carve a palm and the scar is there for the life of the tree. Worse, all of a palm's growth comes from one bud at the very top. Break that bud and the palm does not sprout a new one. The tree that shrugs off a hurricane can be killed by a single well aimed blow to the head.

6.title: The Tree That Bends in the Storm
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Tree That Bends in the Storm

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Family Arecaceae, about 2,600 species
Monocots: cousins of grass, corn, and lilies
No cambium means no rings and no age record
Palms need the coldest month near 41F or above
Palm pollen has been cored from Arctic Ocean mud
The Eocene Arctic had no ice cap at all

blocks.prompt: The Palm Pollen at the Top of the World
blocks.text: A palm tree is a bad historian of its own life and an excellent witness to everything else. Consider what it cannot do. An oak keeps a diary. Every year a living layer under its bark, the cambium, lays down a fresh ring of wood, wide in a kind year, narrow in a dry one, so a stump is a readable record of a century of weather. A palm has no cambium and lays down no rings. It thickens once, near the ground, then rises at that same width for the rest of its life, all its growth pouring out of a single bud at the top. Ask a palm how old it is and it has no answer. Now consider the one thing it says loudly. Palms cannot take a hard frost. The reason is the same missing machinery. With no cambium, a palm cannot grow new tissue over freeze damage, and with only one growing bud, it cannot afford to lose it. Ice ruptures the water filled bundles inside the trunk and the wound stays open forever. So palms live, almost without exception, where the cold months stay above freezing. That is a strict rule, and a strict rule is exactly what a scientist wants, because it can be run backward. If you find a palm, you have found a place that did not freeze. That is why the pollen matters. Drill into the floor of the Arctic Ocean, pull up a core of mud, and count down through the layers to about fifty million years ago, and you will find palm pollen near the top of the world. Do the same off the coast of Antarctica and palm pollen turns up there too, alongside the pollen of tropical trees. The obvious objection is continental drift, and it is the right objection to raise. Continents move. But when geologists reconstruct where those rocks actually sat fifty million years ago, they were still polar. The palms were not somewhere warm that later drifted north. They grew at the poles. The Earth of that time, called the Eocene, held far more carbon dioxide in its air than ours does. There were no ice caps at either end. Crocodile relatives swam in Arctic swamps. And the palms stood through something no palm alive has ever faced: months of continuous winter darkness, in which the sun does not clear the horizon at all. Warm, but pitch black. How they managed it is still argued over. Notice the trade the palm has made. The oak, with its rings, can tell you about one dry summer in 1934. The palm can tell you nothing about itself, not even its age. But because it refuses to grow anywhere that freezes, a single grain of palm pollen in Arctic mud carries a claim an entire ice sheet cannot: that the top of the world was once a place where a palm could grow. The tree that keeps no record turns out to be the record.

answers: (original one-sentence summary: palms keep no record of their own age, but because they cannot survive frost their fossil pollen proves the poles were once warm)
(no cambium to grow tissue over freeze damage and only one bud to lose; cite: Ice ruptures the water filled bundles inside the trunk and the wound stays open forever)
(cite: The obvious objection is continental drift, and it is the right objection to raise; answering the strongest counterargument shows the conclusion survives it)
(cite: A palm tree is a bad historian of its own life and an excellent witness to everything else; supported, because the passage shows it cannot report its age but can report the climate)
(it turns the palm's weakness into its value and closes the paradox opened in line one; earned, because the frost rule and the pollen evidence were both established first)
